findings.claim: Six worksheet items are decided by text the learner sees before answering, not by the topic page. Each item and the text that decides it: (1) service_calls.listening_on_127_0_0_1 (decisions.yaml line 62): the Dockerfile TODO (starter/reviews/Dockerfile lines 4-5) and the test 23 message on the phase 1 run (tests/lab.mjs line 198). This is the only task that elicits the "explain" part of adding-fastapi-service-to-compose#o3. (2) service_calls.httpx_with_timeout_none (line 66): the main.py docstring (lines 33-34) and the test 24 message on the first run (tests/lab.mjs line 248). (3) secrets_in_logs.log_redaction_is (line 87): the test 7 message on the first starter run states it (tests/lab.mjs line 491). (4) secrets_in_logs.hide_a_derived_value_by (line 90): test 21's title, printed in every run and in expected/starter-summary.txt line 21, names the mechanism, and only one option contains that name. (5) secrets_in_logs.fork_pull_request_run_receives (line 93): README line 106 states the fork fact, which leaves one option. (6) delivery.github_actions_jobs_run (line 97): the test 3 message on the first starter run states it (tests/lab.mjs line 398). Reproduced by running the shipped starter: the messages for (1)-(3) and (6) and the title for (4) all appear in that output. Items (4) and (5) are two of the items the operator decision added for secrets-in-ci#o2. With them, no tested part of that objective is left for the page to decide (see ops-edu-11). For service-to-service-calls#o2 (the HTTPX default and RestClient items) and jenkins#o1 (the stage-order item), other items still depend on the page alone.
findings.recommendation: Reword the giveaways so they name the rule without the conclusion. The Dockerfile TODO can say the start command uses the development server. The test 3, 7, 23 and 24 messages can point to the page section instead of restating its claim, and the main.py docstring can say the call disables HTTPX's default without describing the result. Retitle test 21 without naming the mechanism. Drop the fork fact from README line 106, or move the optional login-guard note after phase 7. Alternatively, ask these items about a case the starter text does not describe.

findings.claim: reviews-auth-forward accepts any `if authorization` / `if not authorization` / `authorization is None` text as a guard (tests/lab.mjs lines 278-280), whatever the guard does. Reproduced on a scratch copy: replacing the 401 raise with a guard that only prints a message passes all 26, although the call then still sends None as the header value (the TypeError and 500 both round-1 critics verified). A conditional headers expression that sends no Authorization header when none arrived also passes all 26, and it never answers 401. Yet the test title says "a request without one is refused", and README phase 4 rule 1 (line 80) asks for a 401 before the call.
findings.recommendation: Require the guard to refuse: an `if not authorization` (or `is None`) block whose body raises HTTPException with status 401 before the outgoing call. A required header parameter can stay accepted.

findings.claim: There is a new positional regularity in the worksheet. Across the twelve option lists that each serve a single question (decisions.yaml lines 14, 16, 25, 50, 55, 61, 69, 82, 86, 89, 92, 102), the expected option's position follows one simple rule. Under uniformly random placement that pattern has about a 0.2 percent chance. A learner who spots it can rule out options on every single question and answer the two-option ones outright. The positions were computed by the critic from the public tests and are kept out of this report.
findings.recommendation: Place each single question's expected option uniformly at random (for example with a seeded shuffle kept in private staging), and check the public worksheet for positional regularities before the next critic round.

findings.claim: The worst case is back-fitted rather than derived. worstRequiredBasis (coding-lab-timing.json line 76) adds exactly 60 - 56 = 4 failed reruns at about 1 minute each, and the typical path already assumes no failed run besides the checkpoint and final runs. The decide-* rules report only the first wrong field per run (firstWrong, tests/lab.mjs lines 512-517), so four slips among the 41 worksheet fields, or four across all 26 tests, use up the whole margin. The README repeats the figure as "The worst case" (line 33). It is a typical-with-few-slips estimate, not a worst case, and nothing measures how many reruns a novice needs. The record itself says the independent 3-run solve was by an agent, not a learner.
findings.recommendation: Call the figure what it is ("typical plus four reruns"), or derive it from a stated per-group retry rate. To make retries cheaper, have each decide-* rule report every wrong field in one run.

findings.claim: The committed solved-run record describes the private reference solution beyond what the lab contract allows. coding-lab-solved-run.json line 29 lists solution 1's concrete choices for the start command, the environment style, the timeout object and its arguments, the guard, the handler order, the login technique and the basis of the push expression. authoring/docs/lab-contract.md section 8 (lines 66-71) says validation records only "solved at <commit> by run <id>", and the operator decision requires that no protected solution material enters Git or reports. None of it is a worksheet answer, but it is a partial description of the reference solution in a committed public record.
findings.recommendation: Reduce the solution 1 entry to its provenance, as the solution 2 entry already does, and regenerate the module lock.

items.note: Resolved. The starter call now passes timeout=None (main.py line 41), and docstring rule 2 (lines 33-34) says that turns every limit off, which matches the rule on service-to-service-calls/artifact.md line 41. The README no longer has the troubleshooting line that referred to a timeout=None the starter lacked, and test 24 rejects timeout=None with a message that agrees with the page (tests/lab.mjs line 248). Starter, docstring, README and page now describe the same behaviour.

Open on acceptance clause 2 ("fails when the refused-connection handler does not raise 502/503"). The two cases the original reproduced are fixed. On a scratch copy with the critic's own 26/26 solution and LAB_PROJECT, swapping the two statuses fails test 26. A RequestError handler placed before the TimeoutException handler also fails test 26, with a handler-order message (tests/lab.mjs lines 309-313). Each status is now read from its own except body (handlers(), lines 285-302). The order check covers only the timeout handler, though. The refused-connection handler is picked as any handler after it that names ConnectError, NetworkError, TransportError or RequestError (line 314), even when an earlier handler already catches the exception. Reproduced, each passing all 26: (a) a tuple handler that catches TimeoutException and ConnectError together and answers the timeout status, with the old ConnectError handler left below it as dead code; (b) an `except Exception:` handler answering 500 between the timeout handler and the ConnectError handler; (c) the same with `except httpx.HTTPError:`. In httpx 0.28.1, ConnectError subclasses NetworkError, TransportError, RequestError, HTTPError and Exception (checked with __mro__ in a scratch venv). A Python check of shape (b) returns the catch-all's status for a refused connection. So in all three, a refused connection gets a status the page does not allow, yet test 26 passes. Also, a tuple handler alone (with no separate ConnectError handler) fails with "instead of letting the exception escape" (line 315), although the exception is caught and only its status is wrong. Fix: take the refused-connection handler to be the first handler in source order that catches ConnectError (by name or through a superclass, or a bare except), require it to answer a status the page allows, and word the message about the status.

Open. Inverted and always-true push expressions now fail when the workflow is also triggered by pull requests (reproduced), but ci-build-push skips the pull-request case entirely when no pull_request trigger is listed (tests/lab.mjs line 411). Reproduced on a scratch copy: an on: trigger that lists only push, with the starter's unconditional push value (ci.yml line 25) left unchanged, passes all 26; an always-true expression on github.ref passes the same way. That is the shortest path the starter messages lead to: test 1 says "make it run for every pushed commit" (line 379), and README phase 6 (lines 97-106) never mentions the push condition or building pull requests. The acceptance ("fails inverted or always-true forms") is not met, and on that path the "only built versus also pushed" clause of github-actions-pipeline#o3 is never decided by the learner. Fix: evaluate the pull-request case regardless of the trigger list (or require a pull_request trigger, as the page's on: block shows), and have README phase 6 say that pull requests are built but not pushed.

Open. The env-routed shell form now fails (reproduced: env PW from secrets plus echo "$PW" | base64 fails test 7; a job-level env printed with echo also fails). But refersTo (tests/lab.mjs line 436) only recognises shell $VAR and ${VAR}, not the env context expression. Reproduced: the shipped debug step (ci.yml lines 19-20) kept with its name, given step env REGISTRY_PASSWORD mapped from secrets.REGISTRY_PASSWORD and its run text changed from the secrets context to the env context, passes all 26. GitHub documents the env context as available in jobs.<job_id>.steps.run, so that run prints the secret. The acceptance says the shipped debug step cannot survive by moving its secret into env; it can. Fix: treat ${{ env.NAME }} for a secret-bound NAME the same as $NAME in ci-no-secret-prints (and in ci-secret-refs).
